content: Studies have identified several challenges in HIV testing services (HTS) that compromise the quality of testing. These include issues such as improper specimen collection, incorrect execution of test procedures, misinterpretation of test results, and reading results outside the recommended time frame. Additionally, inadequate supervision and poor management of testing kits have led to stock shortages and the use of expired or damaged rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). In some cases, testing was conducted by inadequately trained staff who lacked understanding of critical concepts, such as the window period for testing, retesting after discrepant results, and verifying HIV diagnoses before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Few testing sites participated in external quality assessment (EQA) schemes, and poor record-keeping, data collection, and transcription errors were common. One study reported that nearly 30% of errors resulted in incorrect test results. Challenges were also noted in interpreting weak reactive test lines, which were sometimes misread as negative results. Implementing quality management systems (QMS) is essential for all forms of HTS, whether conducted in laboratories, health facilities, community settings, or through self-testing. QMS applies regardless of the type of assay used (e.g., RDTs or immunoassays) or the personnel conducting the testing (e.g., laboratory professionals, healthcare workers, lay providers, or self-testers). QA focuses on preventing errors and ensuring that quality requirements are met proactively. QC verifies that products meet quality standards and identifies defects, making it more reactive in nature. QI involves proposing solutions to enhance quality and reliability, often using the plan–do–check–act cycle. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidance on QI in its policy brief, Maintaining and improving quality of care within HIV clinical services. QMS emphasizes the quality of testing processes, not just the quality of the diagnostic product itself. Engaging all individuals involved in the testing process—such as procurement staff, supervisors, testing providers, and clients—is critical. Proper record-keeping and documentation also play a significant role in maintaining testing quality. A high-quality testing service requires not only reliable products but also proper usage, availability, and accessibility of services. At the national level, certain aspects of QMS must be addressed, including the development of national policies, strategic plans, and monitoring processes to support QMS at testing sites. Workforce development is crucial, ensuring that testing providers are adequately trained and supervised. Accreditation of testing sites is also important to uphold quality standards. At the testing site level, QMS principles must be applied to all HIV testing services, whether facility-based or community-based. Site supervisors should be trained in QMS principles, and all testing services should have a quality policy addressing key aspects such as organization, personnel, equipment, inventory management, QC, information management, documentation, occurrence management, assessment, process improvement, client service, and safety. These elements are particularly relevant for sites using RDTs. For HIV self-testing, certain QMS elements, such as personnel and client service, may not apply. However, a common quality policy can be developed for similar testing sites, ensuring that policies and procedures are accessible to all staff. Testing services should be organized to meet community needs, minimize client wait times, and create a stigma-free environment. Quality should be an integral part of all staff roles and responsibilities, rather than a one-time activity. In South Africa, the Rapid Test Continuous Quality Improvement (RTCQI) initiative, supported by WHO and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), has improved HIV testing quality through digital tools. These tools include mobile apps for data collection, real-time dashboards for data analysis, and e-learning platforms for training. Since the launch of the digital version of the Stepwise Process for Improving the Quality of HIV Rapid Testing (SPI-RT) checklist, significant improvements in facility ratings and tester competency have been observed. This digital approach has the potential to be applied to other point-of-care testing services across the continent. Regulation of IVDs is critical for ensuring the quality of HIV testing. WHO’s prequalification process assesses IVDs for safety, performance, and quality, including a review of the manufacturer’s quality management system and independent evaluations. National regulatory authorities (NRAs) can rely on WHO prequalification outcomes to streamline their own registration processes. Post-market surveillance is also essential, requiring manufacturers to monitor product performance and address any quality or safety issues. Testing providers play a key role in identifying and reporting product problems, which should be communicated to NRAs and manufacturers for investigation and corrective action. National policies should support the procurement of verified products, and forecasting should be coordinated across all implementing partners to prevent stock-outs. Community-led monitoring can help address supply chain issues and improve service quality. National accreditation bodies assess sites for compliance with quality standards, such as ISO 15189. Moving toward accreditation within tiered testing networks can enhance the overall quality of HIV testing services. WHO provides guidance on this process through partnerships. In summary, ensuring the quality of HIV testing services requires a comprehensive approach involving national policies, workforce development, regulation of diagnostics, effective supply chain management, and site-level quality management.
